title_en: The French Political Crisis That's Turning Into a Debt Crisis
title_zh: 从政治危机到债务危机：法国困局（嘉宾 Shahin Vallée，German Council on Foreign Relations）
subtitle_zh: 法国政治极化令 2027 大选前景不明，市场担忧债务危机重演，ECB 却难出手兜底。
summary_zh: 本期 Odd Lots 中，Tracy Alloway 与 Joe Weisenthal 请来 German Council on Foreign Relations 高级研究员、曾任 Emmanuel Macron 经济顾问的 Shahin Vallée，讨论法国如何从一场政治危机滑向潜在的债务危机。与 2011—2015 年针对希腊等「欧洲外围」（peripheral Europe）的欧元区危机不同，这次焦点落在向来被视为「核心欧洲」的法国：其债券收益率失控，市场担忧 Mario Draghi「不惜一切代价」（whatever it takes）式的兜底难以重演。Vallée 剖析政治极化——2027 大选前景不明，中间派几近消失，Marine Le Pen 与极左的 Mélenchon 从两端夹击，而 Mélenchon 可能成为法国版的 Varoufakis、以对抗市场赢取政治资本。他复盘了欧元区危机 1.0 遗留的制度补丁：主权—银行「末日循环」（sovereign-bank doom loop）、银行联盟（banking union）与央行充当最后贷款人（lender of last resort）。他还反思 Macron 废除财富税的政治代价，主张法国需要一次专家委员会式的财政规则共识作为「熔断器」，并触及 AI 时代对资本征税的必要性——是一集理解欧元区危机 2.0 风险的深度对话。

turns.zh: 新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Lots Podcast. I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Allaway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: Tracy, I don't know about you, but, uh... I don't think we need another euro crisis right now. Like, we have a lot going on on our plate these days. There's a bunch of stuff to be anxious about, a lot of moving things. The last thing we need is to be talking about European bond spreads yet again.
turns.zh: Tracy，我不知道你怎么想，但呃……我觉得我们现在真不需要再来一场欧元危机。要知道，我们眼下已经够忙的了。有一堆让人焦虑的事儿，很多都在变动之中。我们最不需要的，就是又一次去讨论欧洲债券利差（bond spreads）。

turns.en: And yet, and yet, here we are.
turns.zh: 可即便如此，即便如此，我们还是走到了这一步。

turns.en: Well, we have no choice, right? It's right there. Well, the other thing I.
turns.zh: 唉，我们别无选择，对吧？它就摆在那儿。呃，还有一件事我……

turns.en: Was thinking, so the first eurozone crisis was sort of, I guess, 2011 to 2015, 2016.
turns.zh: 在想，第一场欧元区危机大概是，我想，2011 年到 2015、2016 年那会儿。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: I can't decide if that feels like it was ages ago or just yesterday.
turns.zh: 我真说不清那到底是感觉像很久以前，还是就像昨天的事。

turns.en: I would go with ages ago. I mean, there's so much that's happened since then. And it all seems like not only does it seem like a long time ago, sort of in clock time and how much has happened, seems a little quaint in the sense of like, OK, there is these spreads and Greece, et cetera. Then it was kind of solvable. Margot Draghi came out and said whatever it takes and that they were there to close spreads and stuff. And then it more or less went away. There were some referendums and stuff like that. But like it was a tractable problem and they did ultimately fix it compared to some of the big sort of seismic questions that we seem to be dealing with today.
turns.zh: 我会选很久以前。我是说，从那以后发生了太多事。这一切不仅感觉像是很久以前——无论是从实际时间跨度还是从发生了多少事来看——甚至还有点古早的味道，就是那种，好吧，当时有这些利差、有希腊之类的问题。那时候还算能解决。Mario Draghi 站出来说了那句「不惜一切代价」（whatever it takes），说他们就是要来收窄利差之类的。然后问题就差不多消失了。中间也有一些公投之类的。但那终究是个能处理的问题，他们最后确实解决了，这跟我们今天面对的那些天翻地覆的大问题比起来，真是不一样了。

turns.en: It got fixed. And if you look at Greek bond yields now, which were, you know, the epicenter of the original Eurozone crisis, I mean, they've recovered enormously. And now the key difference, this is a sort of classic history doesn't repeat, but maybe it does rhyme thing. The country or the Eurozone member that everyone is worried about now is one that was viewed as relatively strong just 15 years ago, and that is France. French bonds no longer the GOAT. Did you get that? Oh, come on.
turns.zh: 它确实被解决了。如果你现在看看希腊债券收益率——它可是当初欧元区危机的震中——我是说，它们已经大幅回升了。而现在的关键区别，这是一种典型的「历史不会重演，但也许会押韵」的情况。现在大家都担心的那个国家、那个欧元区成员，恰恰是 15 年前还被视为相对强势的一个，那就是法国。法国债券不再是「史上最佳」（GOAT）了。你 get 到这个梗了吗？哦，拜托。

turns.en: GOAT.
turns.zh: GOAT。

turns.en: Like oats?
turns.zh: 像燕麦（oats）那个？

turns.en: G-O-A-T.
turns.zh: G-O-A-T。

turns.en: Yeah, that's good. Like oats.
turns.zh: 嗯，这个不错。像燕麦那个。

turns.en: Okay, let me do something easier. French bond yields are out of control. There we go.
turns.zh: 好吧，我换个简单点的。法国债券收益率已经失控了。这总行了吧。

turns.en: Oh, that's a good one. That I definitely get.
turns.zh: 哦，这个好。这个我肯定 get 到。

turns.en: The good thing about it being France is that you have a lot more opportunities to make puns.
turns.zh: 事情出在法国，好处就是你有更多机会玩双关。

turns.en: That's right. We should have plenty of opportunities. I used to speak French, by the way, and then I forgot it. The first euro crisis was about peripheral Europe. And so Greece was sort of seen as the worst, but Cyprus also had a very rough time, and Italy and Spain, et cetera. Portugal had some dicey moments, et cetera. This is like much different. And as you're right, like the country that everyone is honed in on is France right now. Core Europe always perceived during the first euro crisis a little bit weaker than Germany, which is core core, but still like by and large, one of the relatively safer ones. And it's also not as straightforwardly about debt, right? There are debt concerns, there are deficit concerns. But also like there are some like deep political concerns.
turns.zh: 没错。我们应该有的是机会。顺便说一句，我以前会说法语，后来忘了。第一场欧元危机是针对欧洲外围（peripheral Europe）的。所以希腊被看作最糟糕的，但塞浦路斯也过得很艰难，还有意大利、西班牙等等。葡萄牙也有一些凶险的时刻，等等。这次就很不一样了。你说得对，现在所有人聚焦的国家是法国。法国属于核心欧洲（core Europe），在第一次欧元危机时，它一直被看作比德国——那是核心中的核心——稍弱一点，但大体上仍是相对安全的那一类。而且这次也不那么单纯是债务问题，对吧？有债务担忧，有赤字担忧。但还有一些深层次的政治担忧。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: We're going to talk about that. But I think a big, just simple part of the story is when people look at the election that's coming up in 2027, they do not see much prospect for like a sort of like centrist Macron-esque campaign. type of candidate. And I think they're worried about like who's going to be running the country in a few months.
turns.zh: 我们会谈到这个。但我觉得，这个故事里一个很关键、也很简单的部分是，当人们看向即将在 2027 年举行的选举时，他们看不到有什么前景会出现一个中间派、类似 Macron 那种路线的候选人。我觉得他们担心的是，几个月之后到底会是谁来掌管这个国家。

turns.en: So this is always my question when it comes to debt crises, because often you see that the fiscal fundamentals, they're kind of the same for ages and ages and ages. I don't think France has run a budget surplus for the entirety of our lives, right? Like this has been the French debt story for ages. So I'm always very curious what the actual catalyst is for people to start getting worried about these things and for yields to actually start shooting up.
turns.zh: 说到债务危机，这一直是我的疑问，因为你常常会看到，财政基本面（fiscal fundamentals）长年累月都差不多。我觉得法国在我们这辈子里就没跑出过预算盈余，对吧？这一直就是法国的债务故事。所以我一直很好奇，到底是什么催化剂，让人们开始为这些事情担忧、让收益率真的开始飙升。

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.en: Well, anyway, even though we do not need another Euro crisis right now, we have no choice. We have to talk about what's going on. And we really do have the perfect guest. We're going to be speaking with Shaheen Vallee. He's a senior fellow at the German Council on Foreign Relations. He's an advisor to institutional investors. He once was an advisor to Macron when he was an economy minister. This was in 2014, 2015. Even advised him on his campaign for a while in 2016 before parting ways before the actual vote in 2017. So someone who really, like I said, the perfect guest. So Shaheen, thank you so much for coming on the podcast.
turns.zh: 好了，无论如何，尽管我们现在并不需要再来一场欧元危机，但我们别无选择。我们必须聊聊正在发生的事。而我们这次真的请到了最合适的嘉宾。我们将要和 Shahin Vallée 对话。他是德国对外关系委员会（German Council on Foreign Relations）的高级研究员。他为机构投资者提供咨询。他曾经是 Macron 的顾问，那时 Macron 还是经济部长，那是在 2014、2015 年。2016 年他还一度为 Macron 的竞选出谋划策，后来在 2017 年正式投票前分道扬镳。所以正如我说的，这真是一位再合适不过的嘉宾。Shahin，非常感谢你来上我们的播客。

turns.en: Thank you for your invitation.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们的邀请。

turns.en: Why don't you give us a little bit of background? Tell us about the time when you were an advisor to current President Emmanuel Macron. What capacity was that? What role was he in at that time? What were you doing for him?
turns.zh: 你先给我们讲讲背景吧？说说你给现任总统 Emmanuel Macron 当顾问的那段时间。那是什么身份？他当时是什么角色？你为他做些什么？

turns.en: So I first met Macron in 2012. I had just joined the cabinet of Hermann von Rompuy, the president of the European Council, who I was advising. And Macron was my counterpart because he was advising President Hollande at the time. And so we've spent... A good two years, the second mandate of President Van Rompuy, working very closely on a lot of actually euro crisis issues from Cyprus to Greece and others. And so when he was appointed minister in the fall of 2014, which also coincided with the end of the mandate of Van Rompuy, I joined him in Paris, in Bercy. And I worked with him primarily on... on European issues, on European economic issues. And the Greek crisis at the time was still in the background. This was just a few months before Syriza and Greece got to power. And I actually knew Varoufakis from a previous life. And I actually introduced Emmanuel Macron and Varoufakis. They actually got along very well. And Macron, I think, did as much as he could to try and help Greece during this pretty pivotal moment. I think he was one of the few French politicians who really understood what was going on and who tried as much as he could to help. But I think the situation in Greece got out of hands, and then the rest is history. But I think it's interesting to be reminded of Greece today, because I think some of the debates that I see emerging in France really remind me of these moments. In particular, I think some of the arguments that are being made by La France Insoumise, for instance, around what can we or cannot do with France's debt, really remind me of some of the arguments that Varoufakis was making at the time and that he sort of, you know, went headfirst in a confrontation with the Eurogroup first and then with the ECB, which ended pretty badly. And I worry that people from La France Insoumise have not learned that lesson yet. and may be heading for the same confrontation. I doubt Jean-Luc Mélenchon will be the next president, so we may be spared that confrontation, but I think it still lingers in the background. And maybe when we talk about politics, I'll say more about this, but I think that's an important setup to be reminded of.
turns.zh: 我是 2012 年第一次见到 Macron 的。那时我刚加入 Herman Van Rompuy 的班子——他是欧洲理事会（European Council）主席，我做他的顾问。而 Macron 是我的对口，因为他当时在给 Hollande 总统做顾问。所以我们花了……整整两年时间，也就是 Van Rompuy 主席的第二个任期，非常紧密地一起处理很多欧元危机议题，从塞浦路斯到希腊等等。所以当他在 2014 年秋天被任命为部长时——那也正好赶上 Van Rompuy 任期结束——我就跟着他去了巴黎，到了 Bercy（法国财政部所在地）。我主要和他一起处理……欧洲事务、欧洲经济事务。当时希腊危机还在背景之中。那是在 Syriza 在希腊上台前几个月。其实我早年就认识 Varoufakis。而且是我把 Emmanuel Macron 和 Varoufakis 介绍认识的。他们其实相处得非常好。我觉得在那个相当关键的时刻，Macron 已经尽全力去帮助希腊了。我认为他是少数几个真正理解当时局势、并竭尽所能提供帮助的法国政界人士之一。但我觉得希腊的局势失控了，剩下的就成了历史。不过我觉得，今天重新提起希腊很有意思，因为我在法国看到浮现出来的一些辩论，真的让我想起那些时刻。尤其是，我觉得比如说 La France Insoumise（不屈法国）提出的一些论点——围绕我们能不能、可以对法国债务做些什么——真的让我想起 Varoufakis 当年的一些主张，他当时可谓一头栽进了先与欧元集团（Eurogroup）、后又与 ECB 的对抗，结局相当糟糕。我担心 La France Insoumise 的人还没吸取那个教训，可能正朝着同样的对抗走去。我怀疑 Jean-Luc Mélenchon 会成为下一任总统，所以我们也许能躲过那场对抗，但我觉得它仍然潜伏在背景里。也许等我们谈到政治时，我会多说一些，但我认为这是一个很重要的铺垫，值得被记住。

turns.en: So we're definitely going to talk about all of that, but why don't we talk about, I guess, the proximate cause of the latest concern? And I decided to fact check what I said in the intro about when France last had a budget surplus. So France hasn't had a budget surplus for more than 50 years at this point, so our entire lifetime. Why are people worried about French debt now?
turns.zh: 这些我们肯定都会聊到，不过我们不如先谈谈，我猜，这一轮担忧的直接诱因？我还特意去核查了一下我在开场时说的、关于法国上一次出现预算盈余是什么时候。结果是，法国到现在已经 50 多年没有预算盈余了，也就是我们整整一辈子。那为什么人们现在开始担心法国债务了？

turns.en: I think they're worried about French debt not because there is anything new about fiscal policy. The budget that was announced is pretty much in line with expectation. In fact, it's probably a touch better than what was expected. I think what has changed in the last few weeks is the perception of the political risk. And I think for two reasons. The first is that I think people have repriced the odds of a centrist candidate getting to the second round. I think for a long time, people assumed that essentially the runoff would be between Marine Le Pen on one end and on the other. some sort of centrist candidate emerging. It was not clear who, but Edouard Philippe was probably the best positioned centrist candidate. And I think what we've seen since the summer is these centrist candidates, pretty much all of them, not only dropping in the polls in the first round, but also, and I think that's probably the more worrying thing, also pretty much now all of them losing in the second round against Le Pen. So I think that's the first change. And as a result... what has emerged as the most likely runoff is a runoff between Marine Le Pen on one hand and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the other. And, you know, one could think that, you know, the polls are so clear about the fact that Marine Le Pen is going to win, that, you know, it's going to win if she is in a runoff versus Mélenchon, I mean, that it shouldn't matter so much. And I think here there's been really something really new in the last few weeks, which is the realization that we're not only looking at a presidential election, we're looking at a presidential election and a month after at a general election. The general election hasn't been called yet. We don't have a date. The next president will likely dissolve the current parliament and call for a new election in order to be able to govern with a new majority. And I think what is emerging now, which I think was not in the picture of most people's mind, is the fact that Marine Le Pen, who was thought to be able to govern with a center-right majority if she needed to, is probably going to face a very difficult general election. So she might well win the presidential election, but she could struggle to actually have a majority in the general election, especially if she's facing a strong far-left opponent like Mélenchon is. And so I think for the first time we have seen emerge the risk that France post these elections in 2027 is actually in a worse place now insofar as being able to decide about fiscal policy than it is today. We're already in a pretty bad place since the elections in 2024 where Macron doesn't have a majority in parliament and therefore has created doubts about passing every budget since. And I think markets were giving the benefit of the doubt to France, assuming that by 2027, we would have a president and a parliament being able to pass a credible fiscal adjustment. And I think we're waking up to the fact that we may not have that. And I think that what most people expected and most people who thought Le Pen could win expected, which is that we would end up with a government that will be in spirit quite similar to the government we've had in Italy since the arrival of Meloni, essentially a center right to the far-right government that has to be fairly pro-European and has to be fairly compliant with European fiscal rules. I think that scenario of a Meloni-like transition is slowly being de-priced. And I think it's right, because I think there are a few reasons why France is not Italy. And I think it's important to unpack that. I think the one thing that is true across Europe is that most of these far-right political parties have indeed stopped being fundamentally anti-European. I think, in fact, they're actually organized around European positions, sometimes more than the mainstream parties. They have a different European agenda. They want a white and Christian Europe for the most part. But they have stopped fighting against the Euro, fighting against the EU. But in France, Le Pen would be in a different position than Meloni because France is a net contributor to the EU budget. And so Le Pen could pick up a fight with the EU on the EU budget, which is actually being negotiated now in a way that I don't think Meloni was in a position to when she arrived in power because Italy was the net recipient of 300 billion of new funds from the recovery and resilience facility. So I think there are several reasons why France and France led by Le Pen could have a much more antagonistic attitude towards the EU and much more difficulty in putting together a coalition than Meloni had.
turns.zh: 我觉得他们担心法国债务，并不是因为财政政策有什么新变化。刚公布的预算基本符合预期。事实上，它可能还比预期稍好一点。我觉得过去几周发生变化的，是对政治风险的认知。我认为有两个原因。第一，我觉得人们重新评估了中间派候选人进入第二轮的概率。长期以来，人们基本上假定，第二轮较量会是一头 Marine Le Pen，另一头是某个浮现出来的中间派候选人。虽然不清楚具体是谁，但 Edouard Philippe 大概是 positioning 最好的中间派候选人。而我觉得，从夏天以来我们看到的是，这些中间派候选人几乎所有人，不仅在第一轮的民调中下滑，而且——我觉得这可能是更令人担忧的——现在他们几乎全都在第二轮对阵 Le Pen 时落败。所以我认为这是第一个变化。结果就是……最可能出现的第二轮对决，变成了一边是 Marine Le Pen、另一边是 Jean-Luc Mélenchon。你知道，有人可能会想，民调已经如此清楚地表明 Marine Le Pen 会赢——如果她进入第二轮对阵 Mélenchon，她会赢——我是说，那这就不该是那么大的问题。而我觉得这里在过去几周出现了一些真正的新东西，那就是人们意识到，我们面对的不只是一场总统选举，我们面对的是一场总统选举，以及一个月后的一场大选（general election）。大选还没被召集。我们还没有日期。下一任总统很可能会解散当前议会、召集新的选举，以便能靠一个新的多数来执政。而我觉得现在浮现出来、但大多数人此前并未纳入考量的一个事实是：Marine Le Pen——原本人们认为她若有需要可以靠一个中右翼多数来执政——很可能将面对一场非常艰难的大选。所以她很可能赢得总统选举，却难以在大选中真正拿到多数，尤其是当她面对像 Mélenchon 这样强劲的极左对手时。因此我认为，我们第一次看到这样一种风险浮现：2027 年这几场选举之后的法国，在决定财政政策的能力上，实际上可能比今天处境更糟。自 2024 年选举以来，我们已经处在一个相当糟糕的境地——Macron 在议会里没有多数，因此此后每一份预算能否通过都打上问号。而我觉得市场原本对法国是往好处想的，假定到 2027 年，我们会有一位总统和一个议会，能够通过一项可信的财政调整。我觉得我们正在醒悟过来：我们未必会有那样的局面。我认为，大多数人、以及大多数觉得 Le Pen 可能获胜的人原本预期的是，我们最终会得到一个在精神上与 Meloni 上台以来意大利政府颇为相似的政府，本质上是一个中右到极右的政府，它必须相当亲欧、必须相当遵守欧洲财政规则。我觉得那个「Meloni 式过渡」的剧本正在慢慢被市场下调定价。而且我觉得这是对的，因为我认为有几个原因说明法国不是意大利，把这层拆开讲很重要。我觉得在整个欧洲都成立的一点是，这些极右政党大多确实已不再从根本上反欧。事实上，我觉得它们甚至是围绕欧洲立场来组织的，有时比主流政党还甚。它们有一套不同的欧洲议程。它们大多想要一个白人的、基督教的欧洲。但它们已经不再与欧元、与欧盟为敌了。但在法国，Le Pen 的处境会与 Meloni 不同，因为法国是欧盟预算的净出资国。所以 Le Pen 可能会就欧盟预算——目前正在谈判——跟欧盟挑起争端，而这是我认为 Meloni 上台时并不具备的处境，因为意大利当时是复苏与韧性基金（recovery and resilience facility）3000 亿新资金的净接收方。所以我觉得有好几个原因，说明由 Le Pen 领导的法国，对欧盟可能采取一种远比 Meloni 更具对抗性的态度，而且在组建联盟上会比 Meloni 困难得多。

turns.en: You know, if we went back 10 or 15 or I guess like 25 years ago when Le Pen's father and the thought that like he would make the runoff, etc., was just like such a shock to all of Europe. I forget who he was running against in 2001 or two.
turns.zh: 你知道，如果我们回到 10 年、15 年、我想大概是 25 年前，那时 Le Pen 的父亲——一想到他会进入第二轮之类——对整个欧洲都是极大的震动。我忘了他 2001 还是 2002 年是跟谁竞选了。

turns.en: Against Schreck in 2002.
turns.zh: 2002 年对阵 Chirac。

turns.en: And that was like such a shock. And now, as you describe it, it's like, OK, like the markets are sort of cool. And it's like I'm with the idea of like Le Pen's coming in. And I was unclear whether it's just has the Overton window shifted, has the quote far right shifted. But what I'm curious about, like, OK, across the West, we've seen the collapse of like centrist or center parties or centrist. Is there anything distinct about France, why the floor has fallen out for the center? Or is it just the exact same thing that we've seen basically everywhere in the Western world, whatever that malaise is, that there's just no appetite for sort of centrism anymore?
turns.zh: 那可真是极大的震动。而现在，照你描述的，就好像，好吧，市场挺淡定的，一副「我接受 Le Pen 上台这个想法」的样子。我搞不清楚，究竟是 Overton window（奥弗顿窗口）移动了，还是所谓「极右」本身移动了。但我好奇的是，好吧，纵观整个西方，我们目睹了中间派或中道政体的崩塌。法国有什么独特之处吗？为什么中间派的地板塌了？还是说这跟我们在整个西方世界基本上到处都见到的一模一样——不管那是种什么病症——就是大家对中间路线（centrism）再没有胃口了？

turns.en: No, I don't think France is unique. You know, I think I've said before that Emmanuel Macron would sadly be our Renzi in Italy, kind of the last force of the center who's trying to hold the center together and who eventually fails to do so. And so very much like Renzi, he's leaving the center, and by that I mean both the center left and the center right, in complete disarray. The Socialist Party had its primary this past weekend in and only 120,000 voted in this primary. In the last presidential election, it was more than a million. So, you know, so I think that says something about the loss of energy, the loss of appetite. And in fact, the real polarization of, you know, I think, politics in most Western countries, but, you know, politics in France in particular, where you actually have now two clear contenders, Le Pen and Mélenchon, coming from, you know, the opposite sides of the political spectrum and pretty much nothing of relevance in the middle.
turns.zh: 不，我不觉得法国是特例。你知道，我以前就说过，Emmanuel Macron 遗憾地说会是我们的 Renzi（意大利那位），算是中道的最后一股力量，试图把中间派维系在一起，最终还是失败了。所以非常像 Renzi，他离开时把中间派——我指的是中左和中右——都留在了彻底的一团乱麻之中。社会党（Socialist Party）上周末举行了初选，只有 12 万人投票。而上一届总统选举时，超过一百万人。所以你知道，我觉得这说明了一种能量的流失、意愿的流失。而且实际上，这也说明了我认为大多数西方国家、尤其是法国政治的真正极化——你现在实际上有两位明确的竞争者，Le Pen 和 Mélenchon，来自政治光谱截然相反的两端，而中间几乎没有任何有分量的东西了。

turns.en: Can you characterize Le Pen's, I guess, fiscal attitude or fiscal stance? Because I see these headlines that, you know, she wants more public spending cuts, but then I also see headlines that are like, oh, and also... We're going to reduce the pension age again, which I always thought was, you know, one of the sources of fiscal weakness in France.
turns.zh: 你能形容一下 Le Pen 的，我猜，财政态度或财政立场吗？因为我看到这些标题说，你知道，她想削减更多公共开支，可我又看到另一些标题说，哦，还有……我们要把退休年龄再降回去，而我一直以为那正是法国财政疲软的一个根源。

turns.en: It's a very important question and a very difficult one because there has been different views expressed by the Rassemblement National on its fiscal policy. I think there's been a turn that was initiated by Jordan Bardella, which was to basically make the party or the political line a lot more fiscally orthodox. And he came up with the possibility of moving the pension age higher. And he kind of gave, I think, all the signals to French businesses and to markets that he could be compatible with a traditional sort of center-right neoliberal economic policy. Le Pen comes from a place where she, I think, is more committed to social spending. She's more committed to protecting pensioners. And so I think she hasn't quite made that U-turn. What's very interesting, however, is that last week, on October 6th, she presented a new and very bold fiscal rule that she would want to introduce in the French Constitution by way of a referendum. And that fiscal rule basically mandates a very significant fiscal adjustment. So she wants to bring the deficit back to the debt-stabilizing deficit. So that's roughly cutting the deficit in half almost immediately. And so long as France is not reaching that debt-stabilizing deficit, she wants to have a minimum of 0.5% of GDP of fiscal adjustment, which is roughly in line with what the European fiscal rules mandate. But the portion that she's introducing is that this would continue basically so long as debt to GDP has not converged back to 60%. So on paper, it's a very strict fiscal adjustment. The governance of it is also extraordinarily tight in the sense that no budget that doesn't meet this rule can be passed. Otherwise, it has to be blocked by the Constitutional Court. And a majority of three-fifths of Parliament... needs to approve a budget that would not respect that rule in the case of an emergency, a recession, a war, an energy crisis. And that can only be done for two years. Otherwise, it has to be approved by referendum. So she's setting the bar in terms of fiscal orthodoxy even higher than the German debt break is setting it. So I think she's understood that it was very important to signal that something strong on fiscal policy. Where I see a bit of cognitive dissonance is that she's saying that, and on the other hand, she hasn't really put the policies that would deliver that kind of fiscal adjustment. So she hasn't said anything substantial on the pension reform, for instance. And so you have a weird situation where she's saying something very bold, and in my view, almost too bold to be credible. on the fiscal front. And she's not backing that with concrete steps to deliver on these promises. And so I don't think that tension is going to be able to survive. At some point, she's going to have to disappoint someone. Either she will have to disappoint markets by saying, actually, what I committed to fiscally, I can't deliver. or she'll have to disappoint her electorate by actually saying, well, my commitment to fiscal orthodoxy means we have to put the pension age back to 65 or plus, for instance. I think that internal discussion inside the Rassemblement National hasn't been settled. It may be settled... during the campaign if fiscal policy becomes a big part of the discussion, and it might, and I think the stress in financial markets might help to propel fiscal discussions at the heart of this campaign. It's striking that even though we're at quite stressed levels in the French spread, fiscal policy hasn't been really at the heart of the policy debate so far. I think it will come, but so far it's been rather timid. And what's interesting is the recomposition that we're seeing around these fiscal issues. Essentially, the center-right all the way to the far-right has basically all embraced some version of a constitutional debt rule. They each have different parameters and different preferences, but more or less, they're all agreeing on that. The left, the Socialist Party and the Greens haven't said anything about this. And La France Insoumise has been very explicitly against it. And so you have a debate that is going to be polarized around the fiscal issue. And what is not clear to me yet is whether that polarization around fiscal issues is not going to actually help La France Insoumise. in the sense that today Mélenchon is out saying very strongly that he's opposed to Le Pen's fiscal rule, that he's the one who is prepared to stand up to markets, that he's the one fighting the governor of the Banque de France or the ECB president around what they're seeing around the French fiscal situation. So it could be that, and this is why I was referring to Varoufakis earlier, It could be that, you know, Mélenchon becomes our Varoufakis and that he gets some political credit for it.
turns.zh: 这是个非常重要、也非常难的问题，因为 Rassemblement National（国民联盟）在其财政政策上表达过不同的看法。我觉得有一个转向是由 Jordan Bardella 发起的，基本上就是让这个党、这条政治路线在财政上正统得多。他提出了把退休年龄往上提的可能性。而且我觉得他向法国企业界和市场释放了各种信号，表明他可以与传统的中右翼新自由主义经济政策相容。Le Pen 的出发点则是，我觉得，她更投入于社会开支。她更致力于保护退休金领取者。所以我觉得她还没完全做那个 U 型转弯。不过非常有意思的是，上周，也就是 10 月 6 日，她提出了一条全新、非常大胆的财政规则，她想通过公投把它写进法国宪法。这条财政规则基本上要求一次非常重大的财政调整。她想把赤字降回到「稳定债务的赤字」（debt-stabilizing deficit）水平。那大致意味着几乎立即把赤字砍掉一半。而且在法国尚未达到那个稳定债务的赤字水平之前，她希望至少有相当于 GDP 0.5% 的财政调整，这大致与欧洲财政规则的要求相符。但她新增的部分是，这基本上会一直持续，直到债务对 GDP 之比重新收敛回 60%。所以纸面上看，这是一次非常严格的财政调整。它的治理机制也异常严格，任何不符合这条规则的预算都无法通过。否则，它必须被宪法委员会（Constitutional Court）拦下。而在紧急情况、衰退、战争、能源危机的情况下，要批准一份不遵守该规则的预算，需要议会五分之三多数……而且那只能维持两年。否则，就必须交由公投批准。所以她在财政正统性上设的门槛，甚至比德国的债务刹车（debt brake）还要高。所以我觉得她已经明白，在财政政策上释放出强硬信号非常重要。而我看到有点认知失调（cognitive dissonance）的地方是，她一边这么说，另一边却并没有真正拿出能实现那种财政调整的政策。比如说，她在养老金改革上就没说什么实质性的东西。于是你看到一种奇怪的局面：她在财政层面说了一些非常大胆、在我看来几乎大胆到不太可信的话，却又没有用具体步骤去兑现这些承诺。所以我觉得这种张力没法长期维持。到某个节点，她必将让某一方失望。要么她得让市场失望，说其实我在财政上的承诺兑现不了；要么她得让她的选民失望，真的去说，好吧，我对财政正统的承诺意味着我们得把退休年龄重新提回 65 岁甚至更高。我觉得 Rassemblement National 内部的这场讨论还没有尘埃落定。它可能会在竞选期间敲定……如果财政政策成为讨论的重头戏的话——而这有可能，我觉得金融市场的紧张或许会助推财政讨论成为这场竞选的核心。令人吃惊的是，尽管法国利差已处在相当紧张的水平，财政政策到目前为止却并没有真正处于政策辩论的核心。我觉得它会来的，但到目前为止还相当畏缩。有意思的是，我们正看到围绕这些财政议题的重新组合。基本上，从中右一直到极右，几乎都接受了某种版本的宪法债务规则。他们各自的参数和偏好不同，但大体上都认同这一点。左翼——社会党和绿党——对此什么都没说。而 La France Insoumise 则非常明确地反对。所以你会有一场围绕财政议题而极化的辩论。而我目前还看不清的一点是，这种围绕财政议题的极化，会不会反而帮到 La France Insoumise。因为今天 Mélenchon 正非常强烈地对外说，他反对 Le Pen 的财政规则，他才是那个准备好对抗市场的人，他才是那个就法国财政状况与 Banque de France（法国央行）行长或 ECB 行长叫板的人。所以有可能——这也是我之前提到 Varoufakis 的原因——有可能 Mélenchon 成为我们的 Varoufakis，并因此获得一些政治资本。

turns.en: What do you mean by that? And tell us a little bit more about Mélenchon, some of the economic things he said. I think he's talked about like canceling French debt. Didn't he also have like he went after the French central banker, etc.? Talk to us a little bit more about those Varoufakis parallels and some of what he said, and then maybe the gap between what he said and what might be realistic.
turns.zh: 你这话是什么意思？再多跟我们讲讲 Mélenchon，讲讲他说过的一些经济主张。我记得他谈过要取消法国债务。他不是还……他还去针对法国央行行长之类的吗？多跟我们讲讲那些与 Varoufakis 的相似之处，以及他说过的一些话，然后再讲讲他说的东西与现实可行之间的差距。

turns.en: The Varoufakis parallel is to illustrate the fact that Varoufakis actually had a lot of political support in Greece and in fact won the referendum that he called for, which was opposing the fiscal adjustment program. And yet he was not able to deliver on the fact that he had won that referendum. And so, you know, I see a strong parallel with what Mélenchon is proposing today, which may get a lot of support, but which I don't think will be very realistic. For instance, you know, Mélenchon is still campaigning, although a bit more quietly these days, on, you know, bringing back the pension age to 60 years old. But what I think he's made most headlines for in the last few weeks is his idea that, you know, yes, the French debt is very high, but in fact, a large portion of that debt, about 20% of it, is owed to the French central bank because the ECB, You know, intervened during both the euro crisis, but also after during the COVID crisis. And as a result, this debt that we owe to ourselves, we could cancel it. So he used a few different expressions, which I think betray very interesting debates that are taking place inside La France Insoumise, but more broadly in economic circles around what is possible with debt monetization and what is not. The first expression he used was the debt that we have at the Banque de France, I will throw it to the fire. I will basically cancel it. And then he used another expression, which was betraying some internal discussions they were having and some changes where he said, you know, instead of throwing it to the fire, he said, I'll put it in the freezer. And by that, he meant instead of canceling it. what we could do essentially is ask the ECB to roll this debt in perpetuity. So instead of eventually this debt maturing and the French government having to roll it and issue that in the bond market, we could basically ask the ECB, in this case the Banque de France, to roll this at infinitum. And it's true that if we did that, That would reduce at the margin the cost of financing France's debt. So he's put this on the table, I think, deliberately to be provocative, not realizing, I think, that this would excite even more market concerns around debt sustainability. And then he became very upset. when the central bankers, and in particular the new governor, Emmanuel Moulin, suggested that this was not really possible, that it would be a violation of European treaties. Moulin had a quote in the Financial Times where he said, I'm worried that France would be strangled by its debt if it doesn't take action to adjust fiscally. And Mélenchon was furious that the governor dared making a reference about France being strangled by the markets and thought this was an act of betrayal. And he actually threatened in a tweet, he threatened the governor of a trial for high treason. So, you know, things got pretty agitated and heated. But I think they exposed the fact that I think Mélenchon' s line is that he's the force that is going to stand to the dark forces of markets. And I think this is where we may have a problem, because if, which I think is actually likely, Mélenchon is in the second round, and if Mélenchon, which I think is very likely too, does very well in the legislative election, we could end up in a situation where Le Pen has won the presidential election, but the parliament, very much like it was after the snap election in 2024, is dominated by the left in general, but the left itself being dominated by Mélenchon, we could be in a pretty ungovernable situation, or at least a situation that would require some kind of compromise between the far left and the far right. And given what I've said earlier, it's really hard to see how that compromise emerges without a much more adult discussion around fiscal policy, which I think we've failed to have in France for quite a while.
turns.zh: 拿 Varoufakis 作类比，是为了说明这样一个事实：Varoufakis 在希腊其实有大量政治支持，事实上还赢得了他自己发起的那场公投——那场公投反对财政调整方案。可他最终无法兑现赢得公投这一结果。所以你知道，我觉得 Mélenchon 今天提出的主张与此高度相似，它可能获得很多支持，但我不认为会非常现实。比如说，Mélenchon 仍在竞选——尽管最近低调了一些——主张把退休年龄重新降回 60 岁。但我觉得他最近几周上头条最多的，是他这样一个想法：是的，法国债务非常高，但实际上这笔债务中有一大部分，大约 20%，是欠法国央行的，因为 ECB 你知道，在欧元危机期间、以及之后新冠危机期间都进行了干预。结果就是，这笔我们欠自己的债，我们可以把它取消掉。他用了好几种不同的说法，我觉得这些说法透露出 La France Insoumise 内部、乃至更广泛的经济圈里正在进行的很有意思的辩论——关于债务货币化（debt monetization）什么是可行的、什么不可行。他用的第一个说法是：我们在 Banque de France 那里的这笔债，我要把它扔进火里烧掉。基本上就是要取消它。然后他又用了另一个说法，透露出他们内部正在进行的讨论和一些变化，他说，与其把它扔进火里，不如我把它放进冰箱冷冻起来。他的意思是，与其取消它，我们本质上能做的，是要求 ECB 把这笔债务永久性地滚动下去。这样一来，就不必等到这笔债务最终到期、由法国政府去滚动它、在债券市场上重新发行，我们基本上可以要求 ECB——在这里也就是 Banque de France——无限期地滚动下去。的确，如果我们那么做，会在边际上降低法国债务的融资成本。所以我觉得他把这个摆上台面，是刻意要挑衅，却没意识到，我觉得，这会进一步激起市场对债务可持续性的担忧。然后他就非常恼火——当央行官员们、尤其是新任行长 Emmanuel Moulin 表示这其实不太可能、这会违反欧洲条约时。Moulin 在 Financial Times 上有句话，他说，他担心法国如果不采取行动进行财政调整，就会被自己的债务活活勒死。而 Mélenchon 对行长竟敢提及法国会被市场勒死感到愤怒，认为这是一种背叛行为。他甚至在一条推文里威胁说，要以叛国罪对这位行长进行审判。所以你知道，事情变得相当激动、相当火药味。但我觉得它们暴露出一个事实：我认为 Mélenchon 的路线就是，他是那股要挺身对抗市场黑暗势力的力量。而我觉得这正是我们可能出问题的地方，因为如果——我觉得这实际上是很有可能的——Mélenchon 进入第二轮，而且如果 Mélenchon——我觉得这也很可能——在立法选举中表现得非常好，我们可能最终陷入这样一种局面：Le Pen 赢得了总统选举，但议会——非常像 2024 年那次提前选举之后的情形——总体上由左翼主导，而左翼本身又被 Mélenchon 主导，我们可能陷入一个相当无法治理的局面，或至少是一个需要极左与极右之间达成某种妥协的局面。而鉴于我之前所说的，很难看出这种妥协如何在没有一场成熟得多的财政讨论的情况下产生——而我觉得，这样的讨论我们在法国已经很久没能进行了。

turns.en: Maybe this is a good point to ask about the French bank. So in Eurozone crisis 1.0, and I'm hoping no more numbers come after that, but in the original Eurozone crisis, one of the worries was we got this sovereign bank doom loop, basically. So, you know, government bonds would sell off. European banks held a lot of those European government bonds and then they would take losses and then weakened banks wouldn't be able to lend. And then eventually, you know, maybe those banks would have to get bailed out by a sovereign, which was already having budgetary pressures of its own. What's the case or what is the current state of French banks? Because I see You know, I get a lot of random analyst notes. I have a lot of French banking analysts who are currently sending things saying French banks are well capitalized. I also saw something interesting, which is that spreads on French bank debt were actually tighter than spreads on the sovereign recently, which is something that you don't see every day. How can we categorize the French banks here?
turns.zh: 也许这正是问法国银行的好时机。在欧元区危机 1.0 里——我希望后面不会再有更多编号——但在最初那场欧元区危机里，其中一个担忧就是，我们基本上出现了这种主权—银行「末日循环」（sovereign-bank doom loop）。就是说，政府债券会被抛售。欧洲银行持有大量这些欧洲政府债券，于是它们会蒙受损失，随后被削弱的银行就没法放贷。然后最终，你知道，也许这些银行将不得不被一个主权国家救助，而这个主权国家自己本就已经承受着预算压力。法国银行是什么情况，或者说它们目前处于什么状态？因为我看到……你知道，我会收到很多零散的分析师报告。我这儿有很多法国银行业的分析师正在发东西说，法国银行资本充足。我还看到一个有意思的现象，就是最近法国银行债务的利差实际上比主权债的利差还要窄，这可不是每天都能见到的。我们该怎么给法国银行归类呢？

turns.en: So the French banks, in comparison, say, to Italian banks or to Spanish banks, have relatively little government debt. So if they were to increase their government debt exposure, they could do that pretty meaningfully and still stay within the bounds of what Italian or Spanish banks do. They have a bit less debt than they did during the euro crisis, at the peak of the euro crisis, but not so few compared to that. So essentially, French debt could increase their exposure to stabilize a bit the market and basically reach the peak that they reached in 2011, 2012. And if they wanted to go very far and go as much as the Italian banks, they would have a lot of space, as much as you know, 300 to 400 billion of space to do that. So I don't think we're in a situation where there is a very active doom loop between the French OAT exposure and the French banks. If you remember, you know, what you said about the euro crisis in 2020, 2011, the moment where there was an acute stress in the French banking system, which actually was, I think, a very critical moment in the summer of 2011, where the crisis stopped being a crisis of the periphery and really became a crisis of the core of Europe. And I think it is, in large part, why Mario Draghi in the summer of 2012 did his famous announcement is because the crisis was moving from the periphery to the core, but it was not so much because of the doom loop at the time in the strict sense, It was because the French had a lot of liabilities and dollars. And in the summer of 2011, essentially the U.S. money market mutual funds stopped financing the European banking system and in particular the French banking system. So basically what really created the crunch on the French banks in the summer of 2011 was the scramble for dollars. we're not in that situation today. And so I'm less worried about a sovereign bank doom loop now than I would have been, you know, 10, 15 years ago.
turns.zh: 法国银行——比方说与意大利银行或西班牙银行相比——持有的政府债务相对较少。所以如果它们要增加政府债务敞口，可以相当可观地增加，同时仍处在意大利或西班牙银行所做的范围之内。它们持有的债务比欧元危机期间、比欧元危机高峰时要少一点，但相比之下也没少太多。所以基本上，法国银行可以增加它们的敞口，来稍稍稳定一下市场，基本上达到它们在 2011、2012 年达到过的那个峰值。而如果它们想走得很远、增加到跟意大利银行一样多，它们会有很大的空间，多达你知道，3000 亿到 4000 亿的空间去这么做。所以我不认为我们眼下处于一种法国 OAT（法国国债）敞口与法国银行之间出现非常活跃「末日循环」的局面。如果你还记得，你知道，你说的那场 2011 年的欧元危机——法国银行体系出现急性紧张的那一刻，我觉得那实际上是 2011 年夏天一个非常关键的时刻，当时危机不再是外围的危机，而真正变成了欧洲核心的危机。而且我觉得，这在很大程度上正是 Mario Draghi 在 2012 年夏天做出那个著名宣布的原因——因为危机正从外围向核心蔓延，但那并不完全是因为当时严格意义上的「末日循环」，而是因为法国人有大量以美元计价的负债。在 2011 年夏天，基本上美国的货币市场共同基金（money market mutual funds）停止了对欧洲银行体系、尤其是法国银行体系的融资。所以基本上，真正在 2011 年夏天给法国银行造成紧逼的，是那场美元荒（scramble for dollars）。今天我们不处于那种局面。所以相比 10 年、15 年前，我现在对主权—银行「末日循环」的担忧要小一些。

turns.en: Can you explain maybe to our listeners who like, Maybe they're young. They don't remember 2011, 2012, and so forth. Can you explain why, in the current environment, it's not as easy for the ECB to sort of put a cap on spreads the way it might have been in Draghi's time?
turns.zh: 你能不能给我们的听众解释一下——他们也许比较年轻，不记得 2011、2012 年那些事了——你能不能解释一下，为什么在当前环境下，ECB 要像 Draghi 时代那样给利差「封顶」，没那么容易了？

turns.en: All they have to do is say whatever it takes, right? Those are the magic words.
turns.zh: 他们要做的不就是说出那句「不惜一切代价」（whatever it takes）吗，对吧？那可是句魔咒。

turns.en: Yeah, why can't they do that this time?
turns.zh: 是啊，为什么这次他们就不能那么说呢？

turns.en: Just say it.
turns.zh: 说出来不就行了。

turns.en: No, it's a very important question because, in fact, we ended the euro crisis because with effectively, without really saying it, a new architecture for the euro area. We essentially departed from the architecture that was written in the Maastricht Treaty to a new architecture that emerged because a few things were added to the euro of the Maastricht Treaty. And these few things were essentially a backstop that allowed to lend to governments, You remember when the euro crisis started, there were a lot of people who said it's actually a violation of the treaty to provide financial assistance to another euro area member state. So we created first the FSF, the FSM, and then the ESM, which actually was kind of a, you can view it as a European version of the IMF, which is basically allowed to lend to countries against an adjustment program. We completed the euro area with what we call the banking union. So essentially a single supervisor for banks and in principle, a single resolution authority precisely to break the doom loop that Tracy referred to between banks and sovereign. And finally, and maybe most importantly, we accepted, without really saying it in so many words, but we accepted that the central bank could be called upon to be a lender of last resort in situations of crisis. And I think what we left Europe with or the euro area with at the time is the impression that we had solidified, we had kind of buttressed the architecture of the euro area and that now we are more robust to crises, which I think is true. That being said, there are some important political conditions attached to that. And these conditions are that we are lending to countries against a fiscal adjustment program. This was the case with most of the countries we referred to. And even the activation of what was called at the time the OMT announced by Draghi was supposed to be only activated... if a country had an ESM program. So basically what the ECB was effectively saying is, I'm prepared to backstop markets. I'm prepared to move markets away from a bad equilibrium towards a good low interest rate equilibrium, provided you're delivering on your part of the job, which is to basically deliver a sound and credible fiscal path. The problem we have today is that we have no signs that France is prepared to deliver on a sound fiscal path. And I think as a result of that, it's very unlikely that the ECB can step in. I think the ECB would have all the power in the world to basically stabilize French debt in a heartbeat. The difficulty is that in order to do that, it needs to see France taking credible long-term steps to consolidate its public finances. And for the reasons that we've talked about before, it's hard to see how politically that can be delivered.
turns.zh: 不，这是个非常重要的问题，因为事实上，我们之所以结束了欧元危机，是因为我们实际上——并没有真正明说——建立了一套欧元区的新架构。我们本质上从写在马斯特里赫特条约（Maastricht Treaty）里的架构，转向了一套新架构，它之所以出现，是因为有几样东西被加进了马斯特里赫特条约所定的欧元体系里。而这几样东西，本质上是一个允许向政府放贷的后备机制（backstop）。你还记得欧元危机开始时，有很多人说，向另一个欧元区成员国提供财政援助其实是违反条约的。于是我们先创建了 EFSF、然后是 ESM，你基本上可以把 ESM 看作欧洲版的 IMF，它基本上被允许在附带一份调整方案的前提下向成员国放贷。我们又用所谓「银行联盟」（banking union）来补全欧元区。本质上就是单一的银行监管者，以及原则上单一的处置机构（resolution authority），恰恰是为了打破 Tracy 提到的银行与主权之间的那个「末日循环」。最后，也许最重要的是，我们接受了——虽然没有明明白白说出口——我们接受了在危机情况下可以要求央行充当最后贷款人（lender of last resort）。我觉得我们当时留给欧洲、留给欧元区的印象是：我们已经巩固、已经支撑起了欧元区的架构，如今我们对危机更有韧性了，我觉得这是真的。话虽如此，这里面附带了一些重要的政治条件。这些条件就是，我们向成员国放贷是以一份财政调整方案为对价的。我们提到的大多数国家都是这种情况。甚至 Draghi 宣布的、当时被称为 OMT（直接货币交易）的那个机制的启动，也应当只在……一个成员国拥有 ESM 方案时才启动。所以基本上，ECB 实际在说的是：我准备好为市场兜底。我准备好把市场从一个坏均衡推向一个低利率的好均衡，前提是你要完成你那部分工作，也就是基本上给出一条稳健、可信的财政路径。我们今天的问题在于，我们看不到任何迹象表明法国准备好去落实一条稳健的财政路径。所以我觉得，正因如此，ECB 出手的可能性非常小。我认为 ECB 完全有能力转瞬间就稳住法国债务。困难在于，要做到这一点，它需要看到法国采取可信的长期步骤来整顿其公共财政。而基于我们之前谈到的那些原因，很难看出这在政治上如何能实现。

turns.en: Yeah, I was just going to say, Tracy, this is the core thing. It's like, okay, we'll backstop your debt if you do this fiscal consolidation. If they could do the fiscal consolidation, we wouldn't be talking about this, period. So it's like, that's the whole ballgame here. And maybe like in 2011, because things were so dire, it's like, OK, there was a perception that governments would. But obviously, if the political will were existed to do that, then we wouldn't even be having this conversation. It's a catch-22.
turns.zh: 是啊，我正要说，Tracy，这就是核心所在。就好比，好吧，如果你做财政整固，我们就给你的债务兜底。可要是他们真能做财政整固，我们根本就不会在这儿讨论了，句号。所以这就是这里的全部关键所在。也许在 2011 年，因为局势太危急了，就好像，好吧，当时有一种看法认为各国政府会去做。但显然，如果真存在那样做的政治意愿，我们甚至都不会有今天这场对话。这就是个「第 22 条军规」式的死结（catch-22）。

turns.en: It's a catch-vendeur.
turns.zh: 这是个 catch-vendeur（把 catch-22 玩成法语的梗）。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，就是这样。

turns.en: It is indeed. But, you know, I think all of these countries in the euro area which had to go through a very tough fiscal adjustment– you know, didn't really, you know, choose it. They were kind of, you know, compelled to by a combination of market forces and political forces in Europe. And I think it's very difficult to explain to these countries that things are going to be very different for France. So my sense is politically, it's very difficult for a German chancellor to allow the ECB to backstop French debt without a severe political cost domestically. And so I think there is, you know, a difficult intra-European political game here. You know, remember that, you know, the biggest threats to the German chancellor today is the rise of the IFD. The IFD was founded as an anti-Euro party, precisely opposing these fiscal, these rescue programs in Greece and others. It has moved since. This is no longer a party that is primarily focused on the euro and it's primarily focused on immigration. But I think for Germany, providing a free backstop to France by way of the ECB is the surest way to increase political support for the AfD, and that's probably not something that this German chancellor can underwrite. So I think we are in a difficult bind, and the ECB, as usual, is in the middle of that political bind.
turns.zh: 确实是。但你知道，我觉得欧元区里所有这些不得不经历非常艰难财政调整的国家——你知道，其实并没有真正去选择它。它们某种程度上是被市场力量与欧洲内部政治力量的合力所迫。而我觉得，很难向这些国家解释说法国的情况将会非常不同。所以我的感觉是，从政治上看，一位德国总理要允许 ECB 为法国债务兜底，而不在国内付出沉重政治代价，是非常困难的。因此我觉得，这里有一盘艰难的欧洲内部政治棋。你知道，记住，今天德国总理面临的最大威胁是 AfD（德国选择党）的崛起。AfD 成立时是一个反欧元政党，恰恰反对希腊等国的那些财政救助方案。它此后已经转向。这已不再是一个主要聚焦欧元的政党，而是主要聚焦移民。但我觉得对德国来说，通过 ECB 给法国提供一个「免费的兜底」，是提升 AfD 政治支持率最确定的方式，而这大概不是这位德国总理能够承担的后果。所以我觉得我们处在一个艰难的两难之中，而 ECB 一如往常，正处在这个政治两难的中央。

turns.en: Can we talk about your time as an advisor to Macron a little bit more? So when I think about ways for governments to raise money in perhaps a politically palatable way, One of those, I would think, would be something resembling a wealth tax, right? Like, you don't want to impose heavier taxes on a bunch of French citizens, the majority of French citizens and workers who are already protesting in the streets. But maybe you could raise taxes on the wealthy, right? And maybe that would be a politically popular way to raise revenue for the government. And yet Macron famously got rid of France's wealth tax. Can you explain the thinking behind there and if the wealth tax could ever come back?
turns.zh: 我们能再多谈谈你给 Macron 当顾问的那段经历吗？当我想到政府或许能以一种政治上容易接受的方式筹钱时，我觉得其中一种，应该就是类似财富税（wealth tax）的东西，对吧？就是说，你不想对一大批法国公民——那些已经在上街抗议的大多数法国公民和劳动者——加更重的税。但也许你可以对富人加税，对吧？也许那会是一种在政治上受欢迎的政府筹钱方式。可 Macron 却以废除法国的财富税而闻名。你能解释一下那背后的思路吗？还有财富税会不会有朝一日卷土重来？

turns.en: So that takes us a long way back to 2016, where I was with a few others indeed advising his campaign. And I disagreed with him precisely on that. So, you know, I thought abolishing the wealth tax was a very bad idea. both symbolically, but also economically. I didn't think it was a good idea to have a less progressive tax system. And I think that costed Macron a lot politically because from that point onwards, he was viewed as or painted as the president of the rich. And I think that undermined a lot of his reform efforts after that. I think he had a very good pension reform in his program in 2017 that he was never able to pass. I think in part because Because I think from that point onward, he was tainted with the suspicion of serving the interest of the rich. So I think that was a mistake. And indeed, I think now there is no way of consolidating public finances without restoring some form of a wealth tax. At minimum, we will return to the wealth tax that we had in 2017 when Macron arrived. But more certainly, we will do more than that. And, you know, France has been really, the French political debate around wealth tax has been really framed by Gabriel Ducman, who is a French economist who is also very influential in the U.S. debate and in the current Californian referendum around taxing billionaires. And he's proposing a very aggressive version of the original French wealth tax. I doubt that we will go as far as the Zucman tax. In fact, interestingly, even Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is advocating for a wealth tax of his own, has not referred or embraced fully the Zucman tax. But I think the wealth tax is an inevitable part of the adjustment process, as well as I think pension reform is an inevitable part of the adjustment process on the spending side. And so I think we have these two sacred cows that we'll probably have to sacrifice in order to deliver any meaningful adjustment over the coming years.
turns.zh: 这就要把我们带回很久以前的 2016 年了，那时我确实和另外几个人一起为他的竞选做顾问。而我恰恰在这一点上和他意见相左。你知道，我觉得废除财富税是个非常糟糕的主意，无论从象征意义上，还是从经济上看都是。我不觉得让税制变得更不那么累进是个好主意。而我觉得这在政治上让 Macron 付出了很大代价，因为从那时起，他就被人看作、或被描绘成「富人的总统」。我觉得这削弱了他此后很多的改革努力。我认为他在 2017 年的纲领里有一项很好的养老金改革，却始终没能通过。我觉得部分原因是……因为我觉得从那时起，他就被「服务于富人利益」的嫌疑所玷污了。所以我觉得那是个错误。而且确实，我觉得如今若不恢复某种形式的财富税，就根本没有办法整顿公共财政。至少，我们会回到 Macron 上台时 2017 年那种财富税。但更有可能的是，我们会做得更多。你知道，法国围绕财富税的政治辩论，其实是由 Gabriel Zucman 塑造的，他是一位法国经济学家，在美国的辩论中、以及当前加州那场关于向亿万富翁征税的公投中也很有影响力。他提出的是原版法国财富税的一个非常激进的版本。我怀疑我们会不会走到「Zucman 税」那么远。事实上，有意思的是，连主张自己那套财富税的 Jean-Luc Mélenchon，都没有提及、也没有完全采纳 Zucman 税。但我觉得财富税是调整过程中不可避免的一部分，正如我认为养老金改革是支出端调整过程中不可避免的一部分。所以我觉得我们有这两头「圣牛」（sacred cows），为了在未来几年实现任何有意义的调整，我们大概将不得不把它们牺牲掉。

turns.en: We hear a lot about, I guess, the sort of China trade question in the context of Germany, and that's huge there. What is the version of that in France these days? And how much similar anxiety is there about, I guess, French industrial giants, et cetera, and their own exposure to surging Chinese exports of higher value, added value goods?
turns.zh: 我们常听到，我猜，是在德国的语境下谈论那个对华贸易问题，那在德国是件大事。如今在法国，这个问题的版本是什么样的？还有，对于法国的工业巨头等等、以及它们自身对不断激增的中国高附加值商品出口的敞口，有多少类似的焦虑？

turns.en: It's a very good question. So the second China shock has been something that the French policy circles have worked on a lot. And I think they have slowly managed to convince Germany that this was a real issue that Europe should act upon. There was a very important Franco-German non-paper on this a week ago, which I think, you know, sort of crystallized this movement of Germany. And there was over the last weekend a deal between the trade commissioner and China, which I think speaks to that willingness of Europe to use more aggressively its trade defense instruments. But economically speaking, I would say France is a lot less exposed than Germany is. To some extent, deindustrialization has occurred in France already. It is occurring now in Germany. And so to some extent, this is a fight that France has already lost. France is a lot more than Germany, fundamentally a service-based economy. The one worry I think that France rightly has is is in the aeronautical business, which remains a very important French export, and one where China is not yet competing, but where it might. The days where the Chinese can produce the equivalent of an Airbus A320 are going to be dark days for Europe and for France. And so I think the worry, even though for the auto sector, which is at the heart now of the fight, you know, there's not a, you know, a central concern for France, the worry is that, you know, that, you know, moves an entire industrial landscape in Europe that could end up, you know, being pretty detrimental to France too.
turns.zh: 这是个非常好的问题。第二次中国冲击（second China shock）一直是法国政策圈下了很大功夫研究的议题。我觉得他们已经慢慢说服了德国，让德国相信这是欧洲应当采取行动应对的一个真问题。一周前有一份非常重要的法德「非文件」（non-paper），我觉得它在某种程度上把德国的这一转向清晰地定型了。而上周末，贸易专员与中国之间达成了一项协议，我觉得这体现了欧洲愿意更激进地使用其贸易防御工具（trade defense instruments）。但从经济上讲，我会说，法国的敞口比德国小得多。某种程度上，去工业化（deindustrialization）在法国已经发生了。它现在正在德国发生。所以某种程度上，这是一场法国已经输掉的仗。法国比德国在更大程度上、从根本上是一个以服务业为基础的经济体。我觉得法国有一个正当的担忧，是在航空业——它仍是法国非常重要的一项出口，也是一个中国尚未参与竞争、但可能会进入的领域。中国人能造出相当于 Airbus A320 那种飞机的那一天，对欧洲、对法国都会是黑暗的日子。所以我觉得，那份担忧在于——尽管对于如今处于交锋核心的汽车业，你知道，那对法国并不是一个核心关切——担忧在于，你知道，它会撼动欧洲整个工业版图，最终可能也对法国相当不利。

turns.en: So in classic debt crises, you often need some sort of circuit breaker to put a stop to the dynamics that are making debt deteriorate and then everyone getting more worried and then the debt deteriorates further, etc. With the original Eurozone crisis, that was the ECB's famous whatever-it-takes statement. What do you see as the most likely circuit breaker for this particular French entanglement?
turns.zh: 在经典的债务危机里，你通常需要某种「熔断器」（circuit breaker），来止住那种让债务恶化、然后大家更担心、债务进一步恶化的动态，如此循环。在最初那场欧元区危机里，那个熔断器就是 ECB 那句著名的「不惜一切代价」表态。对于眼下这一团法国乱局，你认为最可能出现的熔断器是什么？

turns.en: I think we will need two things. One is we will need to have some national consensus emerging on fiscal policy. And, you know, I said some critical words earlier about the German dead break, and I stand by that. I think the German dead break was poorly designed. But I think the good thing that Germany has created was a national consensus on fiscal policy. And it has even now, after this election, actually called upon a commission of experts to try and design the new German fiscal rule. So I think France would need something different. to that effect. Essentially, Macron calling on all the political parties to nominate one or two experts, and for these experts to agree on a consensual debt rule for the next decade. I think we need that kind of political commitment as a first circuit breaker. And I think once we have that, the second circuit breaker is easier to activate. And that's essentially... The ECB, either the OMT, so that takes us back to the framework that you've described during the euro crisis, so essentially some kind of an ESM-like program with OMT interventions, or because there has been a new instrument invented by the ECB since, and that has never been used, the transmission policy instrument, TPI, which can be activated without a program. And I tend to think that this is a more desirable outcome, but it can only be activated if the country in question is deemed compliant with the European fiscal rules. And in order to be compliant with the European fiscal rules, you essentially need what I've described above, which is a political commitment and the political capacity to commit to a fiscal adjustment that is credible over the medium term. So I think the building blocks... for solving this crisis are within reach. And at the same time, I struggle to see how they happen on this side of the French elections. And so it's both, you know, on the horizon. And at the same time, I struggle to see a catalyst now to make the situation better.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们需要两样东西。一是我们需要在财政政策上形成某种全国共识。你知道，我刚才对德国的债务刹车（debt brake）说了一些批评的话，我坚持那个看法。我觉得德国的债务刹车设计得很糟糕。但我觉得德国创造出的好东西，是在财政政策上形成了一种全国共识。而且它现在，甚至在这次选举之后，实际上还召集了一个专家委员会，来尝试设计新的德国财政规则。所以我觉得法国需要某种不同的东西来达到那个效果。本质上就是，Macron 号召所有政党各自提名一两位专家，让这些专家就未来十年的一条共识性债务规则达成一致。我觉得我们需要那种政治承诺，作为第一个熔断器。而我觉得一旦我们有了那个，第二个熔断器就更容易启动了。那本质上就是……ECB，要么是 OMT——这就把我们带回到你在欧元危机期间描述过的那个框架，本质上就是某种类似 ESM 的方案加上 OMT 干预——要么，因为 ECB 后来又发明了一个从未被用过的新工具，即传导保护机制（Transmission Protection Instrument，TPI），它可以在没有方案的情况下启动。而我倾向于认为这是一个更可取的结果，但它只有在相关国家被认定遵守欧洲财政规则时才能启动。而要遵守欧洲财政规则，你本质上就需要我上面所描述的东西，也就是一种政治承诺、以及做出中期可信财政调整承诺的政治能力。所以我觉得，解决这场危机的那些积木……是触手可及的。与此同时，我却很难看出它们如何在法国选举之前这段时间里实现。所以它一方面，你知道，是可望可及的。另一方面，我又很难看到眼下有什么催化剂能让局势好转。

turns.en: Jehanne Vallée, thank you so much. That was an excellent description of what's going on. Really appreciate you coming on Oblots. Maybe we'll talk again around election season.
turns.zh: Shahin Vallée，非常感谢你。你把正在发生的事情讲得非常精彩。真的很感激你来上 Odd Lots。也许到了选举季我们会再聊。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢你。

turns.en: Pleasure. I thought he was great. We covered a lot of ground.
turns.zh: 荣幸之至。我觉得他讲得太棒了。我们聊了很多东西。

turns.en: Yeah, we really did.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们真的聊了很多。

turns.en: You know, I really do think the core thing is that catch-vendue that you identified, or I guess that I identified and you identified as a catch-vendue. It's like, yes, you can have a bailout in exchange for fiscal consolidation.
turns.zh: 你知道，我真的觉得核心就是你说的那个 catch-vendue，或者说是我提出、而你把它定性为 catch-vendue 的那个东西。就好比，是的，你可以拿到一笔救助，代价是财政整固。

turns.en: In exchange for fixing the problem that is necessitating the bailout.
turns.zh: 代价是解决那个正是它导致了需要救助的问题。

turns.en: But if you were going to fix the problem, you wouldn't have needed the bailout in the first place. And so it seems like a real pickle, to say the least.
turns.zh: 但如果你本来就能解决那个问题，你压根就不需要那笔救助了。所以这至少看起来是个真正的难题。

turns.en: It does indeed. I mean, the other thing I keep thinking is there's there's a few ways to get out of a debt crisis, right? I think the one that everyone would prefer is to grow your way out of it. That seems like a long shot in the case of France. The other way is through fiscal austerity, which as we discussed is politically unpopular. Financial repression, which we kind of touched on with the idea of canceling out some of the bonds owed to the ECB. You know, that might be a viable option for a place like France, especially if French banks currently don't hold that much French debt is kind of risky, but it could happen. You can inflate your way out of debt.
turns.zh: 的确如此。我是说，我一直在想的另一点是，走出债务危机有好几种方式，对吧？我觉得人人都更喜欢的那种，是靠增长走出危机。但对法国来说，这似乎希望渺茫。另一种是通过财政紧缩（fiscal austerity），而正如我们讨论的，这在政治上不受欢迎。还有金融抑制（financial repression），我们通过「取消掉一部分欠 ECB 的债券」这个想法多少谈到了它。你知道，对一个像法国这样的地方，这可能是一个可行的选项，尤其是如果法国银行目前持有的法国债务不那么多的话——这有点冒险，但有可能发生。你还可以通过通胀把债务稀释掉。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I feel like sort of all of these are on the table, except maybe serious fiscal austerity.
turns.zh: 我觉得这些选项基本上都摆在桌面上，除了也许严肃的财政紧缩。

turns.en: I don't know.
turns.zh: 我可说不准。

turns.en: Everyone wants a trick, you know, everyone. And arguably, look, someone will get mad at me about saying this, but like arguably even like I think the obsession is not a wealth tax per se. Actually, I think a wealth tax in general is. So in the West, where there is such extreme inequality and so many people have made their money thanks to asset prices and incomes, we're going to at some point, I feel like there has to be more discussion about that. I do think like I'm sort of skeptical that the whole thing can just be solved by like we're going to tax billionaires more, etc., because we would all like to imagine that that would be enough because most of us aren't billionaires, etc., I presume it's all very tricky. What's shocking to me is, I don't know if it's the Overton window or whatever, but I do remember the 2002 Prime Minister, Lionel Jospin, losing in the first round runoff to Jean-Marie Le Pen. And that was just like such an earthquake and obviously a sign of things to come politically in Europe.
turns.zh: 人人都想要一个巧办法，你知道，人人都想。而且可以说，瞧，说这话会有人对我生气，但可以说，甚至我觉得大家的执念并不在于财富税本身。其实我觉得，总体而言财富税是有必要的。所以在西方，那里有如此极端的不平等，这么多人靠资产价格和收入发了财，我觉得到某个节点，关于这一点必须有更多讨论。我确实觉得……我有点怀疑，整件事能不能就靠「我们要对亿万富翁多征税」之类解决掉，因为我们大家都愿意想象那就够了——毕竟我们大多数人不是亿万富翁之类——我猜这一切都非常棘手。让我震惊的是——我不知道这是不是 Overton window 之类的缘故——但我确实记得 2002 年，总理 Lionel Jospin 在第一轮、进入第二轮的角逐中输给了 Jean-Marie Le Pen。那简直就是一场大地震，显然是欧洲政治即将发生之事的先兆。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And now the idea of like, well, if only we could get his daughter Maureen Le Pen in and a stable assembly for her, then we could get like that. She's like firmly within the sort of like normie politics now, which probably speaks to some moderation on her part of the Le Pen family's ideology, but also just like how much has changed that if the sort of Le Pen Maloney style politics like that would be very like acceptable as opposed to investors at this point.
turns.zh: 而现在的想法是，好吧，要是我们能让他女儿 Marine Le Pen 上台、再给她一个稳定的国民议会，那我们就能得到那样一个局面。她现在完全处在所谓「常规政治」（normie politics）的范畴之内了，这可能一方面说明 Le Pen 家族的意识形态在她这里有所温和化，但也说明变化有多大——像 Le Pen、Meloni 那种风格的政治，如今对投资者来说已经变得完全可以接受了。

turns.en: Can I say one thing about the wealth tax?
turns.zh: 关于财富税我能说一句吗？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: You could imagine in a world where AI does more and more of the work, that it's going to be harder for governments to get money out of taxing labor.
turns.zh: 你可以想象，在一个 AI 承担越来越多工作的世界里，政府想通过对劳动征税来筹钱会变得更难。

turns.en: Yeah. Right? No, it's going to be a huge deal.
turns.zh: 对。是吧？不，这会是个大事儿。

turns.en: In which case, you have to tax the capital because the capital is the one generating all the wealth. So I feel like that's going to be I mean, it already is a subject for serious conversation, but perhaps even more so in our AI-powered future.
turns.zh: 那样的话，你就得对资本征税，因为资本才是创造所有财富的那一方。所以我觉得这将会是——我是说，它已经是一个严肃讨论的话题了，但在我们这个由 AI 驱动的未来里，也许会更是如此。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Anyway.
turns.zh: 总之。

turns.en: Anyway, great conversation. I'm glad we did it.
turns.zh: 总之，这是一场很棒的对话。很高兴我们做了这期。

turns.en: Should we leave it there?
turns.zh: 我们是不是就聊到这儿？

turns.zh: 就聊到这儿吧。
